To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the adult mammalian CNS has a remarkable capacity for neurogenesis and plasticity, which may allow for repair of complex neuronal circuits by transplanted precursors and by endogenous precursors that can be induced to produce new neurons.
Transplanted and endogenously generated precursors can be induced to produce new neurons in the adult mammalian central nervous system.

transplanted and, under some conditions, endogenous neural stem cells can differentiate and integrate into appropriate regions of the adult CNS, and that the molecular controls of these events are beginning to be understood.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the repair of complex neuronal circuits by transplanted or resident neural stem cells.
understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which transplated cells and endogenous precursers repair complex neuronal circuitry in the adult brain.
the repair of complex neuronal circuits by transplanted neural precursors, and by endogenous neural precursors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is now sufficient information to conclude that the brain can repair itself, at least to some degree, and that the mechanisms involved in this repair are now beginning to be understood.

there are a number of approaches that can be used to repair neuronal circuits, and that the repair of complex neuronal circuits by transplantation of cells or by recruitment of endogenous neural precursors is possible.
the adult brain is not a fixed, static structure but, rather, is dynamic and plastic and can respond to injury or neurodegeneration by recruiting new neurons from endogenous precursors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the repair of complex neuronal circuits by transplanted or recruited neural precursors is possible.
the repair of complex neuronal circuits by transplanted or by endogenous precursors is a real possibility, and that this possibility may have a major impact on the treatment of CNS disorders.

we have shown that transplanted and/or endogenous neural precursors can be induced to produce new neurons in the adult brain, and that these neurons can integrate into host circuitry and partially repair the injured brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that
endogenous neural precursor cells in the adult brain are not just a curiosity, but can be induced to proliferate and differentiate to partially repopulate regions affected by neuro-degeneration.
endogenous precursors in the adult mammalian CNS are able to respond to injury and disease by producing new neurons and partially repaying damaged regions of the brain.
there is a significant potential for the repair of complex neuronal circuits, including those affected by neurodegeneration, by the recruitment and differentiation of endogenous neural precursors.
